synopsis: HarmoWAM routes a shared video world model into two action experts: inverse-dynamics-style transit control and diffusion-based precise interaction. Real Franka experiments report strong generalization to changed backgrounds, positions and objects, but headline success rates average sub-stages and the implementation remains partly unspecified.

problem.text: Reaching an unfamiliar object and manipulating it precisely can fail for different reasons. In the authors' two-task study, generated-video inverse dynamics reaches targets reliably, whereas a latent-conditioned diffusion policy retains interaction precision when initialized nearby but often fails transit under distribution shift. These particular baselines motivate stage-dependent control; they do not establish a universal division between all WAMs.

contributions.text: A shared Wan world model supplies explicit future frames and implicit dynamics features to complementary Transformer-based action experts.
A visual process classifier selects one expert using interaction labels derived from demonstration events, rather than averaging incompatible action proposals.
The evaluation combines six physical tasks, three controlled distribution shifts, stage-wise measurements and mechanism ablations.

inputs: Natural-language instruction and current RGB observation; experimental observations include multiple camera views and proprioceptive state.
outputs: Future video and video features used internally; executable chunks of relative position, Euler rotation and binary gripper commands, with 7 dimensions per arm and 14 for two arms.

steps.name: Predict visual evolution
steps.detail: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B generates a 13-frame video at 256 × 320 using five denoising steps. Video predictions and latent features condition control; imagined frames are not executable commands.

steps.name: Predictive expert for interaction
steps.detail: A 1B-parameter, 28-block Action DiT denoises action sequences. Cross-attention combines current-step world-model features with SigLIP image features and instruction features. The world feature has shape B × 80 × 3072.

steps.name: Reactive expert for transit
steps.detail: DINOv2-base encodes each predicted future frame into 1369 patch tokens of width 768. Corresponding world features are pooled from 3072 to 768 channels and concatenated along tokens. A convolutional Orientation Decoder maps the fused representation to actions.

steps.name: Route from observed progress
steps.detail: An MLP reuses current-image tokens to predict interaction confidence. Gripper transitions and task-specific height events label interaction windows spanning 20 frames before and after each keyframe; either arm can trigger a dual-arm interaction label.

training.text: Stage 1 fully fine-tunes the world model on task demonstrations with conditional flow matching. Stage 2 freezes it and trains the predictive expert with diffusion noise prediction, the reactive expert with Smooth L1 (beta 0.1), and the gate with binary cross-entropy.

Training uses eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs and 100 demonstrations per task. World-model initialization includes broad robot pretraining: Table 4 lists 201,119 DROID, 3,017 AgiBot and 1,721,985 RoboMIND trajectories; additional closed-source data are mentioned without a count.

inference.text: A confidence above 0.5 selects the predictive expert; otherwise the reactive expert uses predicted frames and future latents. Repeated current-observation feedback supports closed-loop switching. Figure 2's Yes/No branches agree with Section 3.4.

The introduction reports 48 Hz action generation with chunks of 12, while Table 9 reports 4 Hz inference at five world-model steps. Their arithmetic is compatible with chunk throughput, but the source does not establish a 48 Hz observation-to-action replanning loop or specify latency hardware.

equations.explanation: Equation (2): x_1 is a clean demonstration video latent, x_0 is Gaussian noise, xi is the interpolation variable, c contains observation and instruction, and w weights flow steps. The model learns the target velocity x_1 − x_0; the weighting schedule is not specified.
Equation (4) combines action diffusion denoising, reactive Smooth L1 regression and gate binary cross-entropy. Its weights balance these losses while the world model remains frozen.

results.setting: Four single-arm and two dual-arm tasks; 20 independently initialized episodes per task, human stage evaluation.
results.metric: Reported average of task-level sub-stage success rates
results.value: 0.89; authors report ±0.03 standard deviation from three repeated evaluations.
results.interpretation: The displayed differences are 11, 15 and 22 percentage points. These are physical execution results, but 0.89 is not an all-stages-completed episode rate.

results.setting: Same downstream tasks with unseen backgrounds, spatially disjoint object positions, or substitute objects; no OOD fine-tuning.
results.metric: Table 3 Global Avg of task/sub-stage scores across OOD settings
results.value: 0.82 overall; background 0.81, position 0.80, objects 0.85; reported relative drop from ID 7.9%.
results.interpretation: The headline 29 and 33 margins are percentage-point gains over the strongest listed WAM and VLA OOD averages. This tests controlled shifts in familiar tasks, not arbitrary new skills.

results.task: Put Flowers in Vase: final insertion
results.setting: ID dual-arm task, sequential picking, handover and insertion.
results.interpretation: The 0.85 headline flower score averages stages; the harder final insertion succeeds less often.

results.setting: Average over Pick Fruit to Plate and Put Flowers in Vase, position OOD; Figure 5.
results.value: Full model 90; without reactive expert 14; averaging 44; keyframe averaging 59.
results.comparison: Full model exceeds averaging by 46 percentage points and keyframe averaging by 31.
results.interpretation: Routing and the reactive branch matter in this setting. The chart's without-predictive position score is 73, conflicting with 56 in the prose; that disputed value is not treated as resolved.

results.task: Put Flowers in Vase: denoising-step ablation
results.setting: Appendix F.3; world-model denoising budget varied.
results.metric: Reported task success (%) and inference frequency (Hz)
results.comparison: Three: 80%, 4 Hz; ten: 85%, 3.6 Hz; fifty: 87%, 3 Hz.
results.interpretation: Five steps is the authors' speed/quality compromise. The table does not specify an ID/OOD condition, repeated-run uncertainty or inference hardware.

limitations.text: Fixed video horizon limits temporal adaptation, and pixel-level future generation adds overhead. Adaptive horizons and latent-only prediction are proposed future work.
Failures include tilted stacking from placement offsets, vase-rim misalignment after grasp variation, and zipper slippage. The authors attribute the last failure partly to gripper contact mechanics.

Comparisons share downstream demonstrations but not all inputs or pretraining: Wan+AnyPos uses only a third-person view, while others use multiple views. VPP and QwenVLA-OFT omit dual-arm results. Attention images and expert-removal ablations do not independently prove learned physical understanding.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the robot-adapted Wan checkpoint, demonstration data, FR3 arms with UMI grippers, synchronized cameras and stage annotations. Appendix A distinguishes single-arm front/top/wrist views from dual-arm global/two-wrist views, clarifying the compressed main-text camera description.

Unspecified items include closed-source pretraining volume, optimizer and learning-rate schedules, training duration, numeric task height thresholds, exact multi-view fusion, action denoising schedule and execution timing. The architecture is called end-to-end, but the documented action-training stage freezes the world model.

reasoning.text: The shared world model and separately structured diffusion and reactive action experts support the recorded Dual-system interpretation. The reactive branch explicitly maps imagined visual evolution to actions, supporting IDM. The label is incomplete if read exclusively: the predictive branch uses latent-conditioned action diffusion. A single overall framework is not evidence of a single unified action/video backbone.

discussionQuestions: Does routing still help with camera inputs and pretraining held equal across expert baselines?
How sensitive is execution to the interaction-label window and height thresholds?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author/affiliation block and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: Exact title and all eleven authors match the catalog; the inspected artifact is arXiv:2605.10942v1, 11 May 2026. Affiliations are Peking University, Simplexity Robotics and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, with the university laboratory and school named.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 17, Appendix D.1
evidence.detail: Policy conditions on instruction and image; actions comprise relative position, Euler rotation and gripper state, concatenated for two arms. IDM converts video predictions into actions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Table 1 and Section 3.2; p. 18, Appendix D.2
evidence.detail: Ten trials per task/domain/phase compare Wan plus AnyPos with a Wan-conditioned Action DiT. Imagine-then-Execute transit is 10/10 throughout. OOD joint-model interaction entries use near-target initialization, as indicated by asterisks.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.3 and Figure 2
evidence.detail: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B predicts 13 frames at 256 × 320 with five denoising steps; explicit video and latent features feed distinct action experts.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.3, Overall Architecture and World Model to Predictive Expert
evidence.detail: Predictive expert is a 1B, 28-block DiT using image, text and current-step world features, with world features shaped B × 80 × 3072 and cross-attention conditioning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 2 and World Model to Reactive Expert
evidence.detail: DINOv2-base produces B × 1369 × 768 patch features. Future world latents are pooled in channels and concatenated with patch tokens before the Orientation Decoder.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 2; p. 6, Section 3.4 and Equation (1)
evidence.detail: An MLP on current-image tokens predicts interaction probability. Positive interaction labels train BCE; score >0.5 selects predictive, score ≤0.5 selects reactive. Figure branch labels agree.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.5, Equations (2)–(4); p. 17, Appendix C.2, Equations (5)–(6)
evidence.detail: Stage 1 fully fine-tunes the world model with conditional flow matching. Stage 2 freezes it and trains action experts/gate with loss weights 0.1 and 0.05; Smooth L1 beta is 0.1.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 16–17, Appendix C.2 and Table 4
evidence.detail: Eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs are stated. Public robot pretraining counts are DROID 201,119, AgiBot 3,017 and RoboMIND 1,721,985, alongside unquantified closed-source data.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Appendix A and Figure 6
evidence.detail: FR3 arms use 3D-printed UMI grippers. Single-arm cameras are front D435, top D455 and wrist D435, at 640 × 480; dual-arm uses global and two wrist views. Observations also include proprioception.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.1; pp. 15–16, Appendix B and C.1
evidence.detail: Six tasks have 100 SpaceMouse demonstrations each and 20 evaluation episodes per method/task. Stages have task-specific human success criteria. Baselines share downstream data/control spaces; Wan+AnyPos uses a third-person view, unlike multi-view policies. Only selected baselines are tested on dual-arm tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2 caption, Avg column and Section 4.2
evidence.detail: Table 2 explicitly averages critical sub-stages. Global scores are 0.89 HarmoWAM, 0.78 Cosmos-Policy, 0.74 pi0.5 and 0.67 Wan+AnyPos. HarmoWAM has reported ±3% standard deviation over three repeats.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix C.3; pp. 9 and 20, Figures 4 and 9
evidence.detail: OOD backgrounds add 5–8 distractors and alter lighting; test object positions lie in spatially disjoint regions; substitute objects change appearance and geometry.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 3, scenario Avg and Global Avg columns, Section 4.3
evidence.detail: HarmoWAM reports background 0.81, position 0.80, objects 0.85 and global 0.82, with 7.9% relative drop from ID. Global baselines: Wan+AnyPos 0.53, pi0.5 0.49, Cosmos-Policy 0.44.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16, Appendix B, Dual-Arm Tasks; p. 21, Table 6
evidence.detail: Flower stages are pick/handover/insertion, with HarmoWAM 0.95/0.90/0.70; final-stage baselines are 0.40 pi0.5, 0.35 Cosmos-Policy and 0.15 Wan+AnyPos. Bag stages end at 0.80 for HarmoWAM.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 5 panels (a)–(c), legend and Section 4.4
evidence.detail: Two-task ablation plots full HarmoWAM ID/background/position/objects as 93/87/90/90. Position bars are 14 without reactive, 44 averaging, 59 key averaging. Without-predictive position is 73 in the chart but 56 in prose; 56 is the chart's background bar. The -vid suffix removes latent conditioning, not predicted pixels.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 3; p. 6, last paragraph of Section 3.4
evidence.detail: Last-layer attention visualizations contrast reactive attention to gripper/surroundings with predictive attention to manipulated objects; the evidence is qualitative.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 19–20, Appendix D.3
evidence.detail: Gripper changes and task-specific height thresholds create keyframes; 20 frames on either side are labeled interaction. Either arm triggers dual-arm labels. Offline held-out accuracy is 96.95% on 1,637 test frame pairs.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Introduction; p. 23, Appendix F.3 and Table 9; p. 24, Figure 10
evidence.detail: Introduction states 48 Hz action generation and chunk size 12. Flower-task denoising rows give steps/success/frequency: 3/80/4, 5/85/4, 10/85/3.6, 50/87/3. Figure 10 compares generated-video appearance.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 23–24, Appendix G and Figure 11
evidence.detail: Authors discuss tilted stacking, insertion misalignment after grasp variation, and zipper grasp slip, with selected failure images.

evidence.location: PDF p. 25, Appendix I
evidence.detail: Fixed future horizon constrains adaptation; pixel-level generation adds overhead. Adaptive horizon and latent-level prediction remain future work.
